entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sir Otho Holand, alternatively known as Otes or Eton Holand, was a distinguished English soldier and diplomat of the 14th century, best remembered as one of the twenty-six founding Knights of the Most Noble Order of the Garter. Born into a prominent but not initially aristocratic family, his career flourished under the patronage of King Edward III during the tumultuous early decades of the Hundred Years' War. Holand's significance lies in his embodiment of the martial and chivalric ideals of his age, playing a direct role in major military engagements and contributing to the formation of England's highest order of chivalry, which remains a cornerstone of the British honours system.

Holand's military prowess was demonstrated across numerous campaigns in France, notably serving with distinction at the Battle of Crécy in 1346 and the subsequent Siege of Calais, where he was appointed Governor in 1347. His administrative capabilities were also recognized through his appointments as Governor of Guernsey and Jersey from 1353 to 1356. A testament to the perilous nature of medieval warfare, Holand endured capture by the French in 1342 during the Breton War of Succession, necessitating his ransom. He was instrumental in various diplomatic missions, including negotiations for a truce with France, demonstrating a multifaceted contribution beyond mere military command.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Otho Holand's role as a founding Knight of the Garter cemented his place in the enduring history of English chivalry and aristocratic tradition. His military and administrative service significantly supported Edward III's campaigns during the critical early phases of the Hundred Years' War, impacting the geopolitical landscape of Western Europe.
